The objective of this review is to critically examine the available literature in order to explore the hypothesis that endogenous glutathione deficiency may represent a primary pathological condition underlying hyperhomocysteinemia. Glutathione (GSH) is a tripeptide composed of the amino acids glycine, cysteine, and glutamate. GSH primarily serves as a master antioxidant, protecting cells from free radicals and playing a crucial role in maintaining redox homeostasis. Beyond its antioxidant properties, GSH plays a crucial role in numerous cellular processes, making it essential for health and for addressing age-related chronic diseases. The review examines into the redox regulation of homocysteine production and the connection between homocysteine and glutathione metabolism, while also addressing methodological aspects of homocysteine and glutathione measurement and the pre‑analytical and analytical challenges associated with their reliable quantification in clinical settings. It also includes a critical analysis of current experimental HHcy models and their relevance for extrapolation to humans. It is concluded that experimental HHcy is confounded by oxidative stress, a pathological condition that results from, contribute to, or be exacerbated by decreased endogenous glutathione levels. A strong negative correlation between homocysteine and glutathione has been demonstrated, and restoration of endogenous glutathione through nutritional interventions is associated with normalization of blood homocysteine. The literature indicates that the same environmental factors that induce oxidative stress and GSH depletion also activate redox‑sensitive enzymes in the methionine cycle and transsulfuration pathway, thereby driving the metabolic shift toward hyperhomocysteinemia. Consequently, these enzymes facilitate the production of homocysteine and its conversion into cysteine, supplying the rate-limiting substrate essential for glutathione biosynthesis. In this context, hyperhomocysteinemia can be considered an indicator of metabolic reprogramming aimed at restoring disrupted redox homeostasis by supporting glutathione biosynthesis, thereby alleviating oxidative stress and its associated pathological changes. The review concludes by outlining the evidence supporting the view that glutathione deficiency, rather than hyperhomocysteinemia, may constitute the primary underlying abnormality in chronic human diseases. The concept of glutathione depletion as a Trojan horse" challenges the prevailing paradigm that attributes disease pathogenesis primarily to hyperhomocysteinemia. Instead, this condition may be better understood as a risk factor for chronic diseases, given that its underlying mechanisms appear to stem from disrupted redox homeostasis and cellular glutathione deficiency. From a practical standpoint, homocysteine measurement offers a simpler and more accessible laboratory surrogate than direct glutathione assessment for screening individuals with potential GSH deficiency. However, fully realizing the clinical utility of this approach will require further research into the molecular mechanisms by which glutathione depletion drives hyperhomocysteinemia. Elucidating these mechanisms could open genuine and cost‑effective opportunities for the prevention and treatment of chronic diseases by shifting the therapeutic focus from homocysteine to glutathione metabolism.

title: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy as a tool for monitoring treatment-related neurofunctional changes in posttraumatic stress disorder and trauma-related symptomatology: a narrative review.
abstract: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterized by substantial heterogeneity in symptom presentation, illness trajectory, and treatment response, highlighting the need for objective approaches capable of monitoring treatment-related neurofunctional changes beyond conventional symptom-based outcomes. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is an increasingly used non-invasive neuroimaging technique that enables repeated assessment of cortical hemodynamics in clinically feasible settings. Although fNIRS has been widely applied to characterize neurofunctional alterations associated with PTSD, its potential role in monitoring longitudinal treatment-related brain changes has not been critically synthesized. A narrative review was conducted using a structured search strategy across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Library to identify studies published up to 30 January 2026. Studies were eligible if they included adults with PTSD or clinically significant trauma-related symptomatology and employed repeated NIRS/fNIRS assessments to evaluate neurofunctional changes associated with pharmacological or non-pharmacological therapeutic interventions. Four studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis. Across the included studies, the non-pharmacological interventions consisted of trauma-focused psychotherapy, attention-based cognitive training, and equine-assisted services. No eligible longitudinal studies evaluating pharmacological treatments using repeated NIRS/fNIRS assessments were identified. Across studies, treatment was consistently associated with modulation of prefrontal cortical hemodynamic activity, although the direction and magnitude of neurofunctional changes varied according to intervention type, experimental paradigm, and methodological approach. Overall, the available evidence supports the feasibility of repeated fNIRS assessment while highlighting substantial methodological heterogeneity and the limited maturity of the current evidence base. Current evidence suggests that fNIRS represents a promising and clinically feasible approach for monitoring treatment-related neurofunctional changes in PTSD and trauma-related symptomatology, particularly during non-pharmacological interventions targeting prefrontal regulatory processes. Rather than replacing established neuroimaging techniques such as functional magnetic resonance imaging, fNIRS should be considered a complementary tool that is particularly suitable for repeated assessments in real-world clinical settings. Future research should prioritize adequately powered longitudinal studies, standardized acquisition and analytical protocols, multimodal neuroimaging approaches, and the inclusion of pharmacological treatment trials to determine the potential of fNIRS as a candidate longitudinal neurofunctional biomarker of treatment response. Not applicable.

title: Low-dose histrelin for ovulation induction in mares: a partially randomized crossover pilot study.
abstract: This partially randomized crossover pilot study evaluated reduced doses of histrelin for ovulation induction in mares and compared intramuscular (IM) administration with pharmacopuncture at the Bai-hui and Yan-chi acupoints. Eleven mares were enrolled, of which nine completed all eight protocols and were included in the analyses. The protocols comprised 250 µg histrelin IM (standard dose), 75 µg IM, 25 µg IM, no intervention, saline at Bai-hui, saline at Yan-chi, 25 µg histrelin at Bai-hui, and 25 µg histrelin at Yan-chi. Ovulation was assessed by transrectal ultrasonography at scheduled examinations until detected, with ovulation within 48 h as the primary outcome. Ovulations first detected at 24 h were excluded from the primary analysis. Ovulation within 48 h occurred in 88.9% (8/9) of observations with 250 µg IM, 87.5% (7/8) with 75 µg IM, 87.5% (7/8) with 25 µg IM, 37.5% (3/8) with no intervention, 50.0% (3/6) with saline at Bai-hui, 100% (9/9) with 25 µg histrelin at Bai-hui, 12.5% (1/8) with saline at Yan-chi, and 87.5% (7/8) with 25 µg histrelin at Yan-chi. Exact 95% confidence intervals were wide, reflecting the small sample size. Exploratory pairwise comparisons with the no-intervention protocol were performed without adjustment for multiple comparisons and should be interpreted cautiously. The findings provide preliminary evidence that reduced histrelin doses, including 25 µg, may induce ovulation within 48 h in mares. However, this study did not demonstrate an advantage of pharmacopuncture over IM administration of the same reduced dose. Larger, fully randomized studies are required to confirm the efficacy of reduced-dose histrelin and determine whether administration at specific acupoints provides any additional effect.

title: Australian Rotavirus Surveillance Program: Annual Report, 2025.
abstract: This report from the Australian Rotavirus Surveillance Program (ARSP) describes the circulating rotavirus genotypes identified in children and adults during the period 1 January to 31 December 2025. In 2025, the ARSP saw a continuation of a high burden of rotavirus disease in the Australian population. During this period, 2,419 faecal specimens were referred to the National Rotavirus Reference Centre (NRRC) for rotavirus G- and P-genotype analysis; of these samples, 2,288 were confirmed as rotavirus positive. This represents the highest number of referred samples and the highest number of positive samples recorded in a single surveillance year in the NRRC's more than 20-year history. Of the 2,288 samples confirmed rotavirus positive, 2,071 (90.5%) were identified as wildtype rotavirus; 215 (9.4%) were identified as the Rotarix vaccine-like strain; and two G1P[8] samples could not be confirmed as wildtype or vaccine-like due to inadequate sequence quality. The equine-like G3P[8] variant was the dominant genotype nationally (87.7%; n = 1,816/2,071). Other genotypes were identified at low frequencies, including wildtype G1P[8] (0.3%; n = 6/2,071), G2P[4] (2.0%; n = 42/2,071), G3P[8] (2.4%; n = 50/2,071), G8P[8] (0.5%; n = 10/2,071), G9P[4] (0.3%; n = 6/2,071), G9P[8] (2.2%; n = 46/2,071) and G12P[8] (0.3%; n = 6/2,071). Genotype distribution was consistent nationally, with equine-like G3P[8] the dominant genotype in all jurisdictions. Consistent with observations in recent years, a small number of samples with unusual genotypes were identified (3.7%; n = 77/2,071). Of these unusual genotypes, the most frequently detected was equine-like G3P[6] which accounted for 26.0% of unusual samples (n = 20/74) and 1.0% of all positive wildtype samples (n = 20/2,071). The high number of rotavirus positive samples received by the program reflected the notifications for rotavirus disease reported to the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance Service (NNDSS). Across Australia, 9,520 notifications were recorded, which is the second highest annual total reported since rotavirus became nationally notifiable in 2018. Outbreaks were reported in the Northern Territory, Western Australia and Queensland. The ability to monitor the genotypes of rotavirus strains causing disease across ages and jurisdictions provides important data to aid in assessing the performance of the national rotavirus vaccination program and to inform public health interventions during outbreaks. The ARSP also provides important data to monitor annual variations in genotypes circulating in the population. Understanding the diversity of genotypes in circulation and the emergence of variants provides important context for any changes observed in disease epidemiology in the community. The ARSP provides diagnostic laboratories with valuable feedback on laboratory data quality by reporting incidences of wildtype, vaccine-like, and/or false positive rotavirus results.

title: Equine asthma - old disease and new concepts.
abstract: Equine asthma is increasingly recognised as a biologically heterogeneous syndrome in which similar clinical manifestations may arise from distinct molecular mechanisms. Although clinical phenotypes have substantially improved disease classification, increasing evidence indicates that molecular endotypes more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms underlying disease heterogeneity. This review summarises current knowledge regarding the pathophysiological mechanisms of equine asthma, with particular emphasis on inflammatory pathways, molecular endotypes, genetic susceptibility, airway remodelling and emerging neuroimmune interactions. Special attention is given to the transition from phenotype-based disease classification towards mechanism-based endotyping and its potential implications for future diagnostics and targeted therapeutic strategies. The review was based on a comprehensive search of the PubMed and Scopus databases using the terms "equine asthma", "diagnostics", "phenotypes", "endotypes", "genetic background" and "neuroimmune pathophysiology". Following predefined selection criteria, 146 publications were included in the review. Current evidence demonstrates that persistent airway inflammation, structural remodelling, genetic background and neuroimmune signalling interact throughout disease progression and cannot be fully explained by clinical phenotypes alone. Improving our understanding of these biological mechanisms will facilitate more precise disease classification and may provide the foundation for future biomarker-guided diagnosis and precision medicine in equine asthma.
